# Spring Boot Web Application using Layered JAR

This runbook packages a simple Spring Boot Web Application into two container
images and compares the effect of copying the application as one executable JAR
versus copying it as Spring Boot layers.

A standard Spring Boot executable JAR contains the application classes, Spring
Boot loader, and dependency JARs in one archive. That is convenient to run, but
it is a poor fit for Docker layer caching: when a small application class
changes, the Dockerfile copies a new JAR, so the image layer containing the
entire archive changes too.

A layered JAR keeps the same executable application but exposes groups of files
that change at different rates. By default, Spring Boot separates dependencies,
Spring Boot loader classes, snapshot dependencies, and application code. A
Dockerfile can then copy stable dependency layers before the frequently changing
application layer. The result is not a different application; it is a container
image layout that lets Docker reuse more unchanged layers across rebuilds.

This example is intentionally focused on one topic: using Spring Boot layered
JARs to improve Docker layer caching. It omits some production-oriented
container concerns, such as running as a non-root user, image signing,
vulnerability scanning, observability, and deployment-specific hardening, so the
layered JAR behaviour remains easy to follow. For a more complete Spring Boot
container example that combines several concerns, see
[all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

This simple application has one endpoint that returns a random quote from its
database.

**Resources**

- [Container Images](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/html/container-images.html)
- [Packaging Executable Archives](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/3.2.4/maven-plugin/reference/htmlsingle/#packaging)

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

- `curl`, used to call the Spring Boot endpoint.

- `jq`, used to format the JSON response returned by the application.

- `tree`, used to inspect generated directories in the walkthrough.

- [Dive](https://github.com/wagoodman/dive), or a similar tool, is optional
  and used only when visually inspecting image layers.

- [Oracle Account](https://profile.oracle.com/myprofile/account/create-account.jspx)
  to access [Oracle Container Registry](https://container-registry.oracle.com/)

- An Oracle Container Registry authentication token stored in
  `~/.ocr/auth-token`, or an equivalent secure way to pass the password to
  `docker login --password-stdin`.

## Build the application

The application is built once and then reused for the local runtime checks and
both container images. This matters because the comparison should isolate the
runtime packaging choice, not a different application build.

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the application

   This confirms that the packaged JAR works before the container steps add
   Dockerfiles and image layers to the picture.

   The application is started in the background for convenience, otherwise the
   subsequent commands need to be executed in another terminal.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the application to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Aristotle",
     "id": 20,
     "quote": "Happiness depends upon ourselves."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Layered JAR

This section continues on the previous section,
[Build the application](#build-the-application), as it takes the JAR file
created there as input to this section. The goal is to inspect the layered
layout before using the same idea in a Dockerfile.

1. (*Optional*) List the layers available

   Please note that this command has changed since
   [Spring Boot 3.3.0](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-3.3.0-M3-Release-Notes#deprecations-in-spring-boot-330-m3).

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djarmode=tools \
     -jar './target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' \
     list-layers
   ```

   This application uses the four default layers.

   ```
   dependencies
   spring-boot-loader
   snapshot-dependencies
   application
   ```

   The layers are configurable. Please refer to section
   [Custom Layers Configuration](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/maven-plugin/packaging.html#packaging.layers.configuration)
   of the Spring Boot documentation for more information about this.

2. Extract the artefacts from the executable JAR file

   The executable JAR file comprises:
   - Dependencies in the form of JAR files
   - Configurations in the form of text files (YAML, properties, and the like)
   - Classes (plain old `.class` files)

   The `extract --layers` command writes each logical layer to a separate
   directory under `./target/extracted`. Keeping the extracted files under
   `./target` makes the runbook repeatable and keeps generated build artefacts
   away from source files.

   Please note that this command has changed since
   [Spring Boot 3.3.0](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-3.3.0-M3-Release-Notes#deprecations-in-spring-boot-330-m3).

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djarmode=tools \
     -jar './target/layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' \
     extract --layers --destination './target/extracted'
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was properly extracted.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/extracted'
   ```

   Spring Boot writes a separate directory for each logical layer. In current
   Spring Boot versions, each layer may contain JAR files rather than only
   expanded class directories.

   Note that there is a different directory for each of the layers.

3. Copy the artefacts

   The extracted artefacts are grouped into layers. This directory structure
   is useful for Docker copy instructions, but it is not the final runtime
   layout. The contents of each layer directory are copied into one application
   directory (`./target/app/`) in the same order used by the Dockerfile.

   Please reference the
   [Dockerfile example](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/container-images/dockerfiles.html)
   in the Spring Boot documentation.

   ```shell
   DESTINATION='./target/app/'
   rm -rf   "${DESTINATION}"
   mkdir -p "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/dependencies/.'          "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/spring-boot-loader/.'    "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/.' "${DESTINATION}"
   cp -R './target/extracted/application/.'           "${DESTINATION}"
   ```

   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 3 './target/app'

4. (*Optional*) Run the application

   The application can still be started with `java -jar` after the layers are
   flattened because the application layer contains the executable application
   JAR and the copied dependency layers are now beside it.

   The application is started in the background for convenience, otherwise the
   subsequent commands need to be executed in another terminal.

   ```shell
   (cd './target/app'
    java -jar layered-jar-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar > './output.txt' 2>&1 &
    echo $! > '../application.pid')
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the application to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Isaac Newton",
     "id": 81,
     "quote": "I can calculate the motion of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Container Image

This section continues from the previous section,
[Build the application](#build-the-application), as it takes the JAR file
created there as input to this section. The two Dockerfiles intentionally use
the same base image and application build so the difference is limited to how
the application content is copied into the image.

1. Build the Layered JAR container image

   This Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build. The builder stage extracts the
   Spring Boot layers from the executable JAR. The final stage copies those
   extracted layers one by one, creating Docker layers that line up with the
   Spring Boot layer model.

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS builder
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   COPY ./target/layered-jar-spring-boot-*.jar app.jar
   RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar 'app.jar' extract --layers --destination 'extracted'

   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   COPY --from=builder /opt/app/extracted/dependencies/          ./
   COPY --from=builder /opt/app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/    ./
   COPY --from=builder /opt/app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
   COPY --from=builder /opt/app/extracted/application/           ./

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

   The order in which the layers are copied is very important as the layers that
   change the least are copied before those that change more frequently. Docker
   can then reuse the dependency and loader layers when only application code
   changes, and rebuild only the later application layer.

   Build the container image and load it into the local docker daemon.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Layered-Jar' \
     --tag 'demo:layered-jar' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

   The first build has to pull the base image and execute all copy steps. The
   benefit appears on later rebuilds, when unchanged lower layers can be reused.

2. Analyse the Layered JAR container image

   List the layers that were added by the Dockerfile.

   ```shell
   docker history 'demo:layered-jar'
   ```

   The history should show separate copy steps for the Spring Boot layers.

   layer.

   ```shell

   ```

3. (*Optional*) Run the Layered JAR application

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --name 'layered-jar' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:layered-jar'
   ```

   Wait for the container to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the container to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Lao Tzu",
     "id": 106,
     "quote": "When I let go of what I am, I become what I might be."
   }
   ```

   Stop the container once ready.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'layered-jar'
   ```

4. Build the Fat JAR container image

   This Dockerfile copies the executable JAR as one file and runs it with
   `java -jar`. It is simpler, but any application change produces a different
   JAR file, so Docker has to replace the whole application copy layer.

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   COPY ./target/layered-jar-spring-boot-*.jar app.jar

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

   The version used for the build below keeps the complete JDK baseline while
   making the artefact path deterministic.

   Build the container image and load it into the local docker daemon.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Fat-Jar' \
     --tag 'demo:fat-jar' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

   This will take a few seconds to build. When compared to the Layered JAR
   version, later rebuilds have less cache granularity because the complete
   executable JAR is copied again whenever its contents change.

5. Analyse the Fat JAR container image

   List the layers that were added by our Dockerfile.

   ```shell
   docker history 'demo:fat-jar'
   ```

   Unlike the Layered JAR approach, the application content is copied as one
   executable JAR layer.

   ```

   <missing>     8 seconds ago           /bin/sh -c #(nop) COPY file:2c3cde69341db3...  56.5MB
   2c630dad489c  2 hours ago             /bin/sh -c #(nop) WORKDIR /opt/app             0B          FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   <missing>     3 weeks ago             CMD ["jshell"]                                 0B          buildkit.dockerfile.v0

   <missing>     3 weeks ago             ENV PATH=/usr/java/jdk-25/bin:/usr/local/s...  0B          buildkit.dockerfile.v0

   <missing>     6 weeks ago             /bin/sh -c #(nop) ADD file:0ba597b37b1062b...  247MB
   ```

   Analyse the container image using Dive.

   ```shell
   dive 'demo:fat-jar'
   ```

   ![Fat JAR Image](./assets/images/Fat%20JAR%20Image.png)

   Compare this image with the layered image. The layered version has more copy
   steps, but those steps match how often the files usually change. The fat JAR
   version has fewer moving parts, but it gives Docker only one application
   layer to cache or replace.

6. (*Optional*) Run the Fat JAR application

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --name 'fat-jar' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:fat-jar'
   ```

   Wait for the container to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the container to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Steve Jobs",
     "id": 156,
     "quote": "Stay hungry, stay foolish."
   }
   ```

   Stop the container once ready.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'fat-jar'
   ```
